overview: Mixtec history connects distinct kingdoms and communities in Oaxaca. Painted books record ruling families whose interests sometimes conflicted. Archaeology adds the work of farmers, householders and craftspeople to histories often centred on dynasties.

periods.title: Kingdoms remembered in painted histories
periods.summary: Later manuscripts preserve genealogies reaching back into this period. They connect marriages, places and rival families, combining political memory with sacred origins.

periods.title: Gold, status and skilled casting
periods.summary: Surviving ornaments from this broad date range show elaborate casting. Their animal forms and moving parts joined visual display with sound; individual objects lack exact production years.

periods.title: Colonial labour and new demands
periods.summary: Spanish encomienda grants imposed new forms of extraction. Colonial cultivation and livestock gradually changed farming alongside continuing local practices.

items.text: At Nicayuhu, archaeologists excavated Postclassic houses beside terraced fields. Stone foundations and repeatedly renewed floors show long use. Rooms around patios included hearths; sloping floors and heated annexes were interpreted cautiously as possible steam baths.

Nicayuhu households used ordinary pottery and stone tools. Obsidian blades were scarce and sometimes reshaped to prolong their working life. The excavated assemblages reveal maintenance and economical reuse alongside the better-known luxury arts.

Lama-bordo terraces trap soil carried by seasonal runoff behind barriers. Nicayuhu’s excavated layers suggest gradual construction and repair. Pérez Rodríguez argues that households could create these productive fields without a royal administration directing every stage.

Pérez Rodríguez’s later interviews document farmers’ detailed knowledge of soils, weather, plants and pests. Households still built, maintained and farmed lama-bordos. Comparison with excavated terraces helps explain this durable farming practice without assuming that ancient labour arrangements were identical to modern ones.

Codex Bodley is a long painted deerskin strip folded into pages. A white preparation layer supported the images, while red bands organised the reading. Its format made relationships among people, places and events visible across successive panels.

Bodley includes genealogies of families that sometimes opposed each other. Pohl treats its selection and arrangement of stories as a historical problem, not a neutral list of kings. Its painting date remains unresolved after 1500 and may be early colonial.

A gold necklace at The Met combines jaguar-tooth-shaped beads with small bells. Artisans modelled delicate loops in wax before casting them in metal. This “false filigree” technique produced intricate links without attaching separate wires afterward.

The necklace’s bells lacked clappers but could strike one another as the wearer moved. Jaguar imagery associated the ornament with power. The Met compares it with an excavated Tomb 7 necklace; the museum’s object is not itself recorded as that tomb find.

Mixtec painters decorated ceramic vessels with animals, deities and geometric designs in several colours. Tripod vessels and cups with shaped supports show that the pot’s structure contributed to its effect as much as its painted surface.

Rattles, scrapers, conch instruments and drums occur in burial assemblages described by the Museo Chileno. Their presence suggests music’s ceremonial importance. These finds preserve instrument types, although they cannot recover a performance’s full sound or meaning.

Spanish rule brought compulsory labour demands and introduced crops and livestock. Cochineal dye and cotton textiles became important colonial products. These changes affected what households made and owed, without replacing every older crop, skill or community relationship.

INPI’s contemporary account describes migrants maintaining ties with their places of origin and taking part in communal responsibilities. This is evidence of continuing, changing Mixtec communities. It should not be used as a timeless description of every preconquest household.

ending.text: Mexica expansion and then Spanish colonial conquest altered the kingdoms’ authority. Encomienda and other colonial demands reshaped work and landholding. Mixtec communities and cultural knowledge continued through these changes; there was no single event that ended the people’s history.
